# Week 4 Phase 3 - Baseline Performance Results

**Status:** BASELINE ONLY. No application code was changed in this phase.
**Project:** `week4_performance_load_testing` (copy of the Week 3 backend, `app/` untouched).
**Primary endpoint:** `GET /tasks` (`?limit=50`) · **Secondary:** `GET /tasks/stats`
**Generated by:** `python scripts/performance/run_baseline.py --datasets 1000,10000 --concurrency 10,25,50 --duration 20s --repeats 2 --warmup 5`

Raw evidence (never hand-edited):
`artifacts/performance/baseline_summary.json`, `artifacts/performance/baseline_1000_tasks.txt`,
`artifacts/performance/baseline_10000_tasks.txt`, `artifacts/performance/query_counts-1000.json`,
`artifacts/performance/query_counts-10000.json`, and one directory per run under
`artifacts/performance/baseline-<tasks>-u<users>-<target>-r<repeat>/`
(raw Locust CSV + HTML + `summary.json` + `run_metadata.json`).

---

## 0. Test conditions (recorded with every run)

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Machine | Windows 11, AMD64, 12 logical CPUs |
| Python / stack | 3.14.3, FastAPI 0.141.1, Starlette 1.6.0, Pydantic 2.13.5, SQLAlchemy 2.0.52, uvicorn 0.52.4 |
| Load generator | Locust 2.46.6 (gevent 26.9.0), closed model, `wait_time between(0.1, 0.5)` |
| Server | **one** `uvicorn app.main:app` process, no `--workers` |
| Database | SQLite file, throw-away per run, `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`, **no WAL** |
| Dataset | deterministic (`seed_dataset.py`), 1 or 10,000 tasks × 1 comment |
| Warm-up | 5 s of unmeasured `GET /tasks` before every measured run |
| Measured duration | 20 s per run, 2 repeats per configuration (24 runs total) |
| Request recorded | the endpoint row only (the Locust aggregate also contains the per-user bootstrap request) |

### Discarded runs (kept on disk, not used in any number below)

* `artifacts/performance/preliminary_no_warmup/` and the `*-aborted/` directories.
  These were measured **before** a warm-up phase was added; repeats disagreed by up to
  10x (e.g. `u50 GET /tasks` 16.8 rps / avg 2160 ms vs 136.9 rps / avg 23.8 ms in the
  same configuration). They are retained as evidence of the start-up transient and are
  **excluded** from every figure in this document.

## 2. OBSERVATIONS (interpretation of the measurements)

1. **Zero failures in all 24 runs** (11,939 requests, 0 failures). The service is stable
   and correct under this load; nothing here is an availability problem.
2. **Throughput saturates while latency explodes.** For `GET /tasks` at 1,000 tasks:
   28.41 → 68.75 → 97.35 rps as users go 10 → 25 → 50, while average latency goes
   9.87 → 25.37 → **152.96 ms** (15x latency for 3.4x throughput). That is the signature
   of a resource ceiling, not of a slow query.
3. **The ceiling is CPU-bound, not database-bound.** API-process CPU rises
   18 % → 58 % → 130 % with concurrency while database time per request stays flat at
   ~0.12–0.25 ms. `psutil` reports >100 % for multi-threaded processes, so 130–169 %
   means roughly 1.3–1.7 cores.
4. **Statement count is flat and dataset-independent** (3 for every `/tasks` variant,
   6 for `/tasks/stats`) at both 1,000 and 10,000 rows. The Week 3 N+1 fix still holds at
   10x the Week 3 benchmark size; there is no query-count regression to fix.
5. **Database cost is negligible for the primary endpoint.** `GET /tasks` spends at most
   ~1.9 % of its time in SQL, and as little as ~0.15 % at 50 users. Any pure index or
   query-plan optimisation is therefore bounded by roughly a 2 % ceiling here.
6. **`/tasks/stats` is the only endpoint where the database matters.** Its DB time grows
   0.813 → 4.054 ms when rows grow 10x, and at 10,000 tasks / 10 users it accounts for
   ~19 % of the request. It issues 6 aggregate statements, four of which scan the table.
7. **Search is the worst per-query database cost**: `?q=burndown` costs 1.431 ms at 1,000
   tasks and 6.604 ms at 10,000 — roughly linear in table size, consistent with the
   leading-wildcard `ILIKE '%…%'` not being able to use an index. Search was not part of
   the concurrency matrix, so no concurrency figure is claimed for it.
8. **Dataset size matters modestly below saturation** (1,000 → 10,000 rows: avg
   9.87 → 13.21 ms at 10 users) but strongly affects the tail at 50 users
   (p95 290 → 540 ms, p99 375 → 2715 ms).
9. **Load-generator caveat.** With `wait_time between(0.1, 0.5)` the closed workload can
   offer at most `users / 0.3` rps: ~33 at 10 users, ~83 at 25, ~166 at 50. Observed
   throughput (28.4, 68.8, 97.4) sits below that ceiling at 10 and 25 users, so **those
   two levels are partly client-limited, not purely server-limited**. Only at 50 users
   (97 rps against a 166 rps ceiling) is the server the clear limiter.

---

## 3. HYPOTHESES (not yet proven — each needs its own experiment)

| # | Hypothesis | What would confirm it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | The dominant per-request cost is **Python-side response construction/serialisation** (50 x `TaskRead.model_validate` + `model_copy` in `crud.to_task_reads`, plus FastAPI `response_model` validation), not SQL. | Compare `GET /tasks?limit=50` against `?limit=1` under identical load. If latency barely moves, SQL and row fetching are excluded and serialisation is implicated. A py-spy/cProfile sample of the live process would confirm. |
| H2 | At high concurrency **GIL contention** across FastAPI's threadpool (the endpoints are `def`, so they run in worker threads) inflates latency instead of adding throughput. | Compare 1 uvicorn process vs N workers under identical client load. If CPU stays ~1.3-1.7 cores and latency stays high, the work is not parallelising. |
| H3 | **`GET /tasks/stats` is limited by repeated whole-table aggregation** (4 counts + 2 group-bys), which is why it degrades with dataset size while `/tasks` does not. | Re-run the stats scenario at 1,000 / 10,000 / 100,000 rows and compare DB ms; if it tracks row count, the aggregates are the cost. |
| H4 | The **`COUNT(*)` in `crud.list_tasks`** (`query.count()`) is a second full scan, needed only to populate the `total` field. | Compare `?limit=50` with and without the count on a large dataset; `query_counts-*.json` already shows a distinct `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT ...)` per request. |
| H5 | Part of the tail latency at 50 users is **environment noise** (SQLite file I/O, OS scheduling on a shared desktop), not application behaviour. | Repeat 5x at one configuration and inspect the spread; the surviving variance in `baseline_10000_tasks.txt` (p95 230 vs 850 ms) suggests this. |

---

## 4. What the evidence does NOT support

* **An index change on `GET /tasks`** - statement count is already minimal and DB time is
  ~1-2 % of the request. No index can recover the 150 ms measured at 50 users.
* **"A cache is obviously needed"** - nothing measured yet distinguishes wasteful repeated
  work from work that is genuinely required per request.
* **Any claim about production capacity** - this is one machine, one process, read-only
  traffic, with think time in the client.
